title: Dual-Functional Substrate-Integrated Accelerometer–Tactile Architecture for Absolute and Differential Motion Artifact Monitoring and Dual-Modality Arterial Pulse Measurement: Part I—Theoretical Analysis
content: Background: while micro/nano-fabricated tactile sensors are widely studied for arterial pulse measurement and waveform reconstruction. motion artifacts (MA) experienced by a tactile sensor is rarely monitored using an integrated reference sensor. Aim: This study introduces a substrate-integrated accelerometer (ACC)–tactile sensor architecture for absolute and differential MA monitoring and dual-modality arterial pulse measurement. As Part I of this work, this paper establishes the theoretical relationships among the arterial pulse, MA, the TCS stack, and the two sensor outputs. Methods: The architecture consists of a tactile sensor containing a structure embedded with a transducer and a rigid substrate, with an ACC attached to the substrate. A two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) model was developed to describe the TCS-stack dynamics under arterial pulse excitation and MA, where MA is quantified by baseline drift (BD) and causes time-varying system parameters (TVSP) in the TCS stack. The governing equations were analyzed to establish relationships among the two sensor outputs, MA, and TCS system parameters and to characterize their effects on arterial pulse harmonics and instantaneous frequency. Results: The ACC measures absolute motion of the sensor substrate, whereas the tactile sensor measures relative motion between the sensor structure and substrate, providing complementary absolute and differential MA measurements. Both outputs contain arterial pulse components because pulse-induced motion is transmitted through the TCS stack. The TCS stack introduces frequency-dependent effects on individual arterial pulse harmonics, while MA leads to both BD and TVSP-induced distortion associated with each harmonic. The difference between the two measured outputs and their measured instantaneous frequency (IF) are explicitly related to the TCS system parameters. Significance: These complementary measurements provide a mechanical basis for identifying TCS system parameters, offering the potential to evaluate the effects of the TCS stack on the true arterial pulse signal and retrieving the true pulse from the measured outputs.
